questions.question: What is Low-Level Design (LLD) and what does an LLD interview expect you to do?

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand LLD is about concrete class design and OOP relationships, not vague architectural diagrams or high-level system components.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing LLD with High-Level Design (HLD) and talking about databases, load balancers, or microservices instead of class structures and methods.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Immediately clarify requirements by asking about scale, edge cases, and core features before jumping into classes—shows you design intentionally, not randomly.

questions.direct_answer: Low-Level Design (LLD) is the process of designing the internal structure of a system component by defining classes, interfaces, their relationships, and interactions. In an LLD interview, you're expected to translate a problem statement (like designing a parking lot or library management system) into a working class diagram with proper object-oriented design principles, showing how objects collaborate to fulfill requirements.

answer_sections.content: LLD sits between HLD (system architecture) and code. You're designing at the class level: what classes exist, what are their responsibilities, how do they interact, what design patterns apply. For freshers, LLD questions test OOP skills and SOLID principles.

items: LLD = class diagrams, interfaces, method signatures, relationships
HLD = system architecture, services, databases, infrastructure
LLD tests: OOP principles, SOLID, design patterns, encapsulation
Typical questions: design a parking lot, ATM, library system, chess game
Output: class diagram and/or Java class skeletons with key methods
Process: requirements → entities → class diagram → refine with patterns

answer_sections.content: Low-Level Design is about translating a real-world problem into classes, interfaces, and their relationships. It's different from high-level architecture which deals with services and databases. In an LLD interview, I'm asked to design something like a parking lot: identify the entities (ParkingLot, Floor, ParkingSpot, Vehicle, Ticket), define their attributes and behaviors, map relationships (a ParkingLot has many Floors, a Floor has many Spots), apply appropriate patterns (Strategy for pricing, Observer for availability updates). The output is a class diagram and often Java class skeletons. It tests OOP thinking, not just coding ability.

speakable_v2.hook: HLD asks 'which services and databases'; LLD zooms all the way in to 'which classes, fields, and method signatures'.

beats.text: Low-Level Design means translating a real-world problem into classes, interfaces, and relationships. It sits between high-level architecture — which covers services and databases — and actual code. In an interview, you're asked to model something like a parking lot as Java classes.
Interviewers use LLD to test your OOP thinking. Anyone can write code; LLD shows whether you can structure it cleanly before you write a single line.

items: Identify entities: ParkingLot, Floor, ParkingSpot, Vehicle, Ticket
Define attributes and behaviors for each class
Map relationships: a ParkingLot has many Floors, a Floor has many Spots
Apply patterns: Strategy for pricing, Observer for availability updates
Deliver a class diagram and Java class skeletons with key methods

beats.text: For a parking lot, you'd model ParkingLot as the top-level class, give it a list of Floor objects, and have each Floor hold a list of ParkingSpot objects. Vehicle is abstract, with Car and Truck as subclasses. That's LLD in action.
candidates miss: jumping straight into code without first identifying entities and relationships. Always say your process out loud so the interviewer can follow along and guide you.

speakable_v2.cap: LLD interviews test OOP thinking — not coding speed. Model your entities, map their relationships, and talk through your reasoning as you go.

sections.title: What Low-Level Design Is
sections.content:
**Low-Level Design (LLD)** is designing the **internal structure of one component**: its **classes**, **interfaces**, their **fields and methods**, and the **relationships** between them. Where High-Level Design (HLD) decides *which services and databases exist*, LLD decides *what classes live inside one service and how they collaborate*.

In an interview you translate a prompt — "design a parking lot" — into a **class diagram** plus key **Java skeletons**, applying OOP principles (encapsulation, inheritance, composition) and a couple of design patterns. The interviewer is watching your *process*, not just the final classes.

sections.title: HLD vs LLD vs What's Tested
sections.content:
blue|HLD|~System-level|services, DBs, APIs|load balancing, scaling|the 30,000ft view
emerald|LLD|~Component-level|classes, interfaces|fields + methods|relationships
amber|What you produce|~In the interview|class diagram|Java skeletons|pattern choices
violet|What's judged|~Your process|clarify first|SRP + relationships|trade-off talk

sections.title: LLD Output — a Class Skeleton
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing LLD with HLD** — talking load balancers and sharding when asked for classes.
- **Jumping to code without clarifying** — always scope the requirements first.
- **Listing classes with no relationships** — the connections are the design.
- **Ignoring OOP principles** — LLD is judged on encapsulation, SRP, and sensible patterns.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **LLD = internal class structure** of one component.
- **HLD** = services/DBs; **LLD** = classes/interfaces/methods.
- Deliverables: **class diagram + Java skeletons + pattern choices**.
- OOP principles (encapsulation, SRP, composition) are the grading rubric.
- Interviewers judge **process**, not just the final classes.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Low-level design is the process of designing the internal structure of a single component — its classes, interfaces, the fields and methods they hold, and crucially the relationships between them. The easiest way to place it is against high-level design. HLD operates at the system level: which services exist, what databases they use, how they talk over APIs, how you scale and load-balance. LLD zooms all the way in to one of those services and asks, what classes live inside it and how do they collaborate.

So in an LLD interview, when someone says design a parking lot or a library system, what they want me to produce is a class diagram and some key Java skeletons — the actual classes with their fields and method signatures — built using object-oriented principles like encapsulation, inheritance, and composition, plus a couple of design patterns where they fit naturally.

The thing I'd emphasise is that the interviewer is watching my process as much as the final answer. They want to see me clarify the requirements first, then identify entities, assign each a single responsibility, map the relationships, and only then reach for patterns. A common mistake is drifting into HLD territory — talking about sharding and caching — when the question is really about clean class structure. Another is jumping straight into writing classes without scoping what we're actually building. LLD is fundamentally about translating a problem into well-structured, maintainable objects.

questions.question: What is the difference between IS-A and HAS-A relationships in LLD?

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of fundamental OOP relationships and knowing when to use inheritance versus composition in class design.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Overusing inheritance for code reuse even when there's no logical IS-A relationship, leading to fragile designs.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the 'favor composition over inheritance' principle and give a concrete example where you'd choose composition to avoid tight coupling.

questions.direct_answer: IS-A represents inheritance where a subclass IS-A specialized type of the parent class (Car IS-A Vehicle). HAS-A represents composition or aggregation where one class HAS-A reference to another (ParkingLot HAS-A list of ParkingFloors). Composition implies ownership and lifecycle dependency, while aggregation implies a weaker relationship. Favor composition over inheritance unless there's a true specialization relationship.

rows: ParkingLot HAS-A Floor (Floor can't exist without lot)

answer_sections.content: IS-A means inheritance — Car IS-A Vehicle, so Car extends Vehicle. HAS-A means an object contains another — a ParkingLot HAS-A list of Floors. HAS-A further splits into composition (the contained object can't exist without the container — a Floor doesn't exist without a ParkingLot) and aggregation (the contained object has independent existence — an Employee exists without a Department). In LLD, 'favor composition over inheritance' is a key principle. Inheritance creates tight coupling and can lead to fragile hierarchies. Composition is more flexible — I can change the pricing algorithm in a ParkingLot by swapping the Strategy without changing the class hierarchy.

follow_up_questions: When would you use inheritance vs composition for a design?
What is the Liskov Substitution Principle and how does it relate to IS-A?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: IS-A or HAS-A is the question that decides extends versus a field — and getting it wrong builds a hierarchy that collapses.

groups.heading: IS-A (Inheritance)
groups.text: Car IS-A Vehicle, so Car extends Vehicle. Use this when the subclass truly is a specialized version of the parent — not just when it shares some fields.

groups.heading: HAS-A Composition
groups.text: A ParkingLot HAS-A list of Floors. The Floor can't exist without the ParkingLot — it's owned. This is composition.

groups.heading: HAS-A Aggregation
groups.text: A Department HAS-A list of Employees, but an Employee exists independently of the Department. That's aggregation — shared, not owned.

beats.text: Prefer composition over inheritance — it's less brittle. Only use inheritance when there's a genuine IS-A relationship, not just shared behavior.
sharp edge: if you find yourself using inheritance just to reuse code, that's a smell. Switch to composition and inject the shared behavior as a dependency instead.

speakable_v2.cap: IS-A is inheritance; HAS-A is composition or aggregation. When in doubt, favor HAS-A — it keeps your design flexible.

sections.title: IS-A vs HAS-A Relationships
sections.content:
**IS-A** is **inheritance**: a subclass is a specialized type of its parent — `Car IS-A Vehicle`, expressed with `extends`. **HAS-A** is **composition/aggregation**: one class holds a reference to another — `ParkingLot HAS-A list of ParkingFloors`.

The deciding question: *"is X genuinely a kind of Y in every context?"* If yes, inheritance. If it's really *"X is made of / uses Y"*, composition. The widely-taught guidance is **favour composition over inheritance** — it's more flexible and avoids brittle, deep hierarchies.

sections.title: IS-A vs HAS-A at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|IS-A|~Inheritance|Car extends Vehicle|a specialized type of|tight coupling
emerald|HAS-A composition|~Owned part|ParkingLot has Floors|part dies with the whole|loose coupling
amber|HAS-A aggregation|~Shared part|Department has Employees|part lives independently|a weaker link
rose|Favour composition|~Default choice|swap parts at runtime|no leaked parent API|inherit only if truly IS-A

sections.title: IS-A vs HAS-A
sections.content:
| Aspect | IS-A (Inheritance) | HAS-A (Composition) |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | Specialized type of | Made of / uses |
| Keyword | `extends` / `implements` | a field reference |
| Example | `Car extends Vehicle` | `ParkingLot` has `List<Floor>` |
| Coupling | Tight (locked at compile time) | Loose (swap at runtime) |
| Reuse | Inherit behaviour | Delegate to the part |
| Guidance | Use when truly IS-A | **Favour this** for reuse |

sections.title: Inheritance misused — IS-A is false
Composition — HAS-A keeps the contract clean
Key Points
sections.content:
- **IS-A** → inheritance (`extends`); **HAS-A** → composition (a field).
- Decide by: *is X a kind of Y in every context?*
- **Favour composition** — looser coupling, runtime flexibility.
- Composition exposes only the intended API; inheritance leaks the parent's surface.
- Deep inheritance hierarchies (4+ levels) are a design smell.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
IS-A and HAS-A are the two fundamental ways classes relate, and choosing between them is one of the most important calls in low-level design. IS-A is inheritance: a subclass is a more specialized type of its parent, so a Car is-a Vehicle, and I express that with extends. HAS-A is composition or aggregation: one class holds a reference to another as a field, so a ParkingLot has-a list of ParkingFloors. Composition usually implies ownership and a shared lifecycle, while aggregation is a looser version where the part can outlive the whole.

The test I apply is to ask whether X is genuinely a kind of Y in every context. If a car really is a vehicle everywhere it's used, inheritance is fine. But if the relationship is really X is made of Y or X uses Y, that's composition. The classic example of getting it wrong is making a Stack extend ArrayList. A stack is not really an array list, and by inheriting you accidentally expose methods like add-at-index that let callers violate the stack's contract. The composition version holds a private list and exposes only push and pop, so the API stays clean.

That's why the standard guidance is to favour composition over inheritance. Composition gives looser coupling and lets you swap the inner part at runtime, whereas inheritance is locked in at compile time and tends to produce brittle, deep hierarchies. I only reach for inheritance when the is-a relationship is genuinely true and permanent.

questions.question: What is the step-by-step process for solving an LLD interview question?

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you follow a structured problem-solving approach rather than randomly throwing classes together without reasoning.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Jumping straight into coding classes without clarifying ambiguous requirements or understanding the problem scope first.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explicitly verbalize each step as you go—say 'Now I'm identifying entities' or 'Let me map the relationships'—shows disciplined thinking.

questions.direct_answer: The standard LLD process has five steps: (1) Clarify requirements and constraints by asking questions, (2) Identify core entities and actors from the problem domain, (3) Define class responsibilities ensuring each class has one clear job (SRP), (4) Map relationships between classes using inheritance, composition, or association, (5) Apply design patterns where they naturally fit and refine the design iteratively.

items: 1. Clarify requirements: what are the use cases? What can users do?
2. Identify entities: nouns in requirements become classes (ParkingLot, Vehicle)
3. Attributes and behaviors: what does each class know and do?
4. Relationships: IS-A (inheritance) vs HAS-A (composition/aggregation)
5. Design patterns: identify where Strategy, Observer, Factory help
6. Review for SOLID: single responsibility? Open for extension?

answer_sections.content: My LLD process: First, clarify requirements — I ask 'what are the key use cases?' and 'any scale constraints?' before touching the design. Second, I identify entities by picking the nouns from the requirements — for a parking lot: ParkingLot, Floor, ParkingSpot, Vehicle, Ticket, Payment. Third, for each entity I define what it knows (attributes) and what it does (methods). Fourth, I map relationships: a ParkingLot has Floors (composition), Vehicle is abstract with Car and Truck subclasses (inheritance). Fifth, I look for design pattern opportunities: pricing strategy that varies by vehicle type → Strategy pattern. Sixth, I review against SOLID principles — am I violating SRP anywhere? I describe this process out loud so the interviewer can follow along and guide me.

follow_up_questions: How do you decide between inheritance and composition in LLD?
What SOLID principles are most commonly violated in LLD and how do you avoid them?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: Five steps, in order: clarify, find entities, assign responsibilities, map relationships, then — and only then — patterns.

beats.text: A structured process lets you tackle any LLD problem systematically. Without it, you'll either freeze or jump to code too fast.

groups.heading: Step 1 — Clarify requirements
groups.text: Ask: what are the key use cases? Any scale constraints? Spend two minutes here before touching the design.

groups.heading: Step 2 — Identify entities
groups.text: Pick the nouns from the requirements. For a parking lot: ParkingLot, Floor, ParkingSpot, Vehicle, Ticket, Payment.

groups.heading: Step 3 — Attributes and behaviors
groups.text: For each entity, define what it knows (fields) and what it does (methods).

groups.heading: Step 4 — Map relationships
groups.text: Decide IS-A (inheritance) vs HAS-A (composition or aggregation) for each pair of entities.

groups.heading: Step 5 — Apply patterns and review SOLID
groups.text: Look for Strategy, Observer, or Factory opportunities. Then check: am I violating Single Responsibility anywhere?

beats.text: non-obvious: the interviewer cares as much about your process as your final diagram. Narrate each step out loud — it signals structured thinking even if the design isn't perfect.

speakable_v2.cap: Clarify, identify entities, map relationships, apply patterns, check SOLID — say each step out loud and you'll stand out.
followup_handoff: How do you decide between inheritance and composition in LLD?
Which SOLID principles are most commonly violated?

sections.title: The 5-Step LLD Process
sections.content:
A repeatable process keeps you calm and structured under pressure. The standard five steps: **(1) Clarify** requirements and constraints, **(2) Identify** core entities and actors, **(3) Define responsibilities** (one job per class — SRP), **(4) Map relationships** (inheritance, composition, association), **(5) Apply patterns** where they naturally fit, then refine.

The order matters: patterns come **last**. Freshers who lead with "I'll use the Observer pattern" before understanding the domain almost always over-engineer.

sections.title: The 5-Step LLD Process
sections.content:
blue|1 Clarify|~Scope first|use cases + scale|edge cases|what's in and out
emerald|2 Identify entities|~Noun-verb scan|nouns -> classes|verbs -> methods|plus actors
amber|3 Responsibilities|~SRP|one job per class|one reason to change|high cohesion
violet|4 Map relationships|~Connect classes|IS-A -> inheritance|HAS-A -> composition|uses -> association
rose|5 Patterns last|~Only if they fit|Strategy/Factory/Observer|refine iteratively|never lead with patterns

sections.title: The Five Steps
sections.content:
| # | Step | What you actually do |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Clarify | Ask about scope, scale, edge cases; pin down what's in/out |
| 2 | Identify entities | Noun-verb analysis → candidate classes + actors |
| 3 | Define responsibilities | One reason to change per class (SRP) |
| 4 | Map relationships | IS-A → inheritance; HAS-A → composition; uses → association |
| 5 | Apply patterns + refine | Strategy/Factory/Observer *only where they solve a real problem* |

sections.title: Steps 2–4 Made Concrete
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Skipping clarification** — designing the wrong thing fast is still wrong.
- **Patterns first** — leading with patterns before understanding the domain = over-engineering.
- **No responsibility check** — entities pile up into God classes without SRP.
- **Treating it as linear** — you'll loop back and refine; that's expected, not a failure.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Five steps: **clarify → entities → responsibilities → relationships → patterns**.
- **Patterns last** — only where they solve a real problem.
- Use **SRP** in step 3 to keep classes cohesive.
- Map **IS-A (inheritance)** vs **HAS-A (composition)** in step 4.
- The process is **iterative** — expect to refine.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
I follow a five-step process, and having it memorised keeps me structured even when the problem is unfamiliar. Step one is clarify: I ask about scope, scale, and edge cases, because designing the wrong thing quickly is still designing the wrong thing. Step two is identify the core entities and actors, which I do with noun-verb analysis — nouns become candidate classes, verbs become methods. Step three is define responsibilities, applying the Single Responsibility Principle so each class has exactly one reason to change, rather than letting one God class absorb everything. Step four is map the relationships: I decide which links are is-a and use inheritance, which are has-a and use composition, and which are plain associations. Step five is apply design patterns where they genuinely fit, and then refine.

The single most important thing about the order is that patterns come last. A really common fresher mistake is to open with I'll use the Observer pattern before even understanding the domain, and that almost always leads to over-engineering — patterns bolted on for their own sake. Patterns should emerge from a problem you've actually identified, like pricing rules that change, which then justifies Strategy.

I'd also stress that the process isn't strictly linear. As I map relationships or apply a pattern, I often discover something that sends me back to adjust the entities or responsibilities, and that iteration is exactly what good design looks like, not a sign I got it wrong the first time.

questions.question: How do SOLID principles apply in LLD design?

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to apply SOLID principles in practical design scenarios, not just recite textbook definitions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Listing SOLID acronym definitions without showing how they influence actual design decisions in the given problem.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through your design and explicitly call out where you applied each principle with concrete examples from your class structure.

questions.direct_answer: SOLID principles guide LLD design: Single Responsibility Principle means each class has one clear purpose (ParkingSpot manages occupancy, not billing). Open/Closed means you extend behavior through subclasses or interfaces, not by modifying existing code. Liskov Substitution means subclasses can replace parent classes without breaking functionality. Interface Segregation means using focused interfaces instead of one fat interface. Dependency Inversion means depending on abstractions like interfaces, not concrete classes.

items: SRP: ParkingTicket generates ticket; PricingCalculator calculates price — separate
OCP: Vehicle is abstract; adding ElectricVehicle doesn't modify existing code
LSP: Car and Truck both extend Vehicle and can be used interchangeably
ISP: Payable interface and Reservable interface — not one big interface
DIP: ParkingLot depends on IVehicle interface, not concrete Car class

answer_sections.content: In a parking lot design, I apply SOLID throughout. SRP: the ParkingLot class knows about floors and availability; a separate FeeCalculator handles pricing — one class shouldn't do both. OCP: I make Vehicle abstract so I can add ElectricVehicle or Motorcycle without changing existing Vehicle or ParkingLot code — open for extension, closed for modification. LSP: Car and Motorcycle both extend Vehicle, and anywhere I use Vehicle in the code, either subclass works correctly. ISP: instead of one big VehicleInterface with all methods, I have separate Parkable and Chargeable interfaces. DIP: ParkingLot stores List<Vehicle> (interface), not List<Car> — it doesn't depend on the concrete type.

How does the Strategy pattern enforce the Open/Closed Principle?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: SOLID isn't five trivia answers — it's five forces that, applied together, keep a class diagram from rotting.

beats.text: SOLID is five principles that keep class designs clean and extensible. In LLD, you're expected to apply them proactively, not just recite their definitions.

groups.heading: SRP — Single Responsibility
groups.text: ParkingLot manages floors and availability; FeeCalculator handles pricing. They don't mix.

groups.heading: OCP — Open/Closed
groups.text: Vehicle is abstract so you can add ElectricVehicle without touching existing code.

groups.heading: LSP — Liskov Substitution
groups.text: Anywhere you use a Vehicle reference, Car or Motorcycle works correctly without surprises.

groups.heading: ISP — Interface Segregation
groups.text: Separate Parkable and Chargeable interfaces instead of one fat interface with all methods.

groups.heading: DIP — Dependency Inversion
groups.text: ParkingLot stores a List of Vehicle (interface), not a List of Car. It depends on the abstraction.

beats.text: candidates miss: SRP is the most commonly violated. It's tempting to add a fee calculation method directly to ParkingLot. Resist it — give that responsibility to its own class.

speakable_v2.cap: Weave SOLID into your design as you talk — don't wait for the interviewer to ask. It's the clearest signal of a strong LLD candidate.

How does the Strategy pattern enforce the Open/Closed Principle?

sections.title: Applying SOLID in LLD
sections.content:
**SOLID** is five design principles that keep object-oriented code maintainable. In LLD they're not a quiz — they shape your classes:

- **S**ingle Responsibility — one reason to change per class.
- **O**pen/Closed — extend via new code, don't modify working code.
- **L**iskov Substitution — a subclass must work anywhere its parent does.
- **I**nterface Segregation — small focused interfaces, not one fat one.
- **D**ependency Inversion — depend on abstractions, not concrete classes.

Applied together they explain *why* you split a God class, use Strategy, and program to interfaces.

sections.title: Java — OCP + DIP in One Example
SOLID in Practice
sections.content:
amber|SRP|~One reason to change|split God classes|FeeCalculator vs Spot|high cohesion
blue|OCP|~Open to extend, closed to modify|new class not edit|Strategy pattern|add WeekendFee
emerald|LSP|~Subtype substitutable|no surprises|Square/Rectangle trap|honour the contract
violet|ISP|~Small interfaces|Payable not IVehicle|implement only what you need|no fat interface
rose|DIP|~Depend on abstractions|inject interfaces|UserRepository|swap impls + test

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reciting SOLID as definitions** — show it in the design (split a class, inject an interface).
- **LSP violations** — a subclass that throws on an inherited method breaks substitutability.
- **Fat interfaces** — forcing implementers to stub methods they don't need (ISP).
- **Depending on concretes** — `new MySqlRepo()` inside a service couples them; inject the interface (DIP).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **S**RP: one reason to change; **O**CP: extend, don't modify.
- **L**SP: subtypes substitutable for parents; **I**SP: small focused interfaces.
- **D**IP: depend on abstractions, inject them.
- OCP + DIP together justify **Strategy** and **programming to interfaces**.
- Demonstrate SOLID **through the design**, not as recited definitions.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
SOLID is five principles that keep object-oriented designs maintainable, and the way to show I understand them is to apply them in the design rather than recite definitions. Single Responsibility says each class has one reason to change, which is why I split a God class into a ParkingSpot that tracks occupancy and a FeeCalculator that handles pricing. Open/Closed says code should be open to extension but closed to modification, so I add a new pricing rule as a new class rather than editing the existing lot. Liskov Substitution says a subclass must be usable anywhere its parent is, without surprises — the classic violation is a subclass that throws on a method it inherited, which breaks any code relying on the parent's contract.

Interface Segregation says prefer small, focused interfaces over one fat one, so I'd define a Payable interface rather than forcing every vehicle to implement a giant IVehicle with methods it doesn't need. And Dependency Inversion says depend on abstractions, not concrete classes, so my ParkingLot takes a FeeCalculator interface in its constructor instead of newing up a specific calculator inside itself.

What I find most useful is that these principles reinforce each other. Open/Closed and Dependency Inversion together are exactly why I program to interfaces and use the Strategy pattern — I depend on an abstraction and extend by adding implementations. So in an interview I don't list SOLID as a checklist; I let it explain why I made each structural decision.

questions.question: What are the most useful design patterns to know for LLD interviews?

interviewer_intent.testing: Pattern recognition—can you identify when a standard pattern solves a recurring design problem rather than inventing solutions from scratch.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forcing patterns into the design where they don't fit, or not recognizing obvious pattern opportunities like using Singleton for a globally shared resource.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the problem each pattern solves before applying it, showing you understand the 'why' not just the 'how'—e.g., 'I'd use Strategy here because pricing rules change frequently.'

questions.direct_answer: The most useful design patterns for LLD interviews are: Singleton for ensuring one shared instance (like ParkingLotManager), Strategy for interchangeable algorithms (different pricing strategies), Observer for event notification (notify users when spots are available), Factory for creating objects without specifying exact class (VehicleFactory creates Car or Motorcycle), Builder for constructing complex objects step-by-step (ParkingLotBuilder), and Decorator for adding features dynamically (adding VIP features to a ParkingSpot).

rows: Only one instance of core system
Create objects without specifying exact class
Complex object with many optional fields

answer_sections.content: For LLD interviews, these patterns come up constantly. Singleton: the ParkingLot or ATM controller should have one instance. Strategy: whenever an algorithm can vary — pricing, search, sort — Strategy encapsulates it so you can swap implementations. Observer: when state changes in one class need to notify others — availability display updates when a spot is filled. Factory Method: when you need to create different subtype objects based on input — creating different Vehicle types based on type string. Builder: when you're constructing complex objects with many optional fields — building a ParkingTicket with optional features. Recognizing when to apply these patterns is the main LLD interview skill.

follow_up_questions: When should you NOT apply a design pattern?
How does the Strategy pattern differ from the Template Method pattern?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot or ATM system
speakable_v2.hook: You don't need all 23 GoF patterns — five carry the vast majority of LLD interviews, and knowing when not to use them matters too.

beats.text: LLD interviews reward pattern recognition: seeing the shape of a problem and knowing which pattern fits. You don't need all 23 GoF patterns — just the six that keep showing up.

groups.heading: Singleton
groups.text: One instance of a core system object. Use for ParkingLot, ATMController — there should only ever be one.

groups.heading: Strategy
groups.text: Swappable algorithms. Use when pricing, search, or sort logic varies — encapsulate each option as its own class.

groups.heading: Observer
groups.text: Notify on state change. Use when a ParkingSpot becoming full needs to update an availability display.

groups.heading: Factory Method
groups.text: Create objects without specifying the exact class. Use when VehicleFactory.create('CAR') should return a Car.

groups.heading: Builder
groups.text: Construct complex objects step by step. Use for objects like ParkingTicket that have many optional fields.

groups.heading: Decorator
groups.text: Add behavior without subclass explosion. Use when a LuxuryParkingSpot adds features to a regular ParkingSpot.

beats.text: gotcha: don't force a pattern where a simpler solution works. Over-engineering a two-class design with unnecessary patterns is a red flag to interviewers.

sections.title: The Patterns That Actually Show Up in LLD
sections.content:
You don't need all 23 Gang-of-Four patterns. Five cover the vast majority of fresher LLD interviews:

- **Singleton** — one shared instance (a `ParkingLot` controller).
- **Strategy** — interchangeable algorithms (pricing, search).
- **Observer** — event notification (spot freed → notify display).
- **Factory** — create objects without naming the concrete class (`VehicleFactory`).
- **Builder** — construct complex objects with optional fields readably.

Know each one's *problem*, a one-line Java sketch, and — just as important — when **not** to use it.

sections.title: Java — Factory + Builder Sketch
Five Patterns, Five Problems
sections.content:
amber|Singleton|~One shared instance|private constructor|getInstance()|don't overuse (global state)
blue|Strategy|~Swap algorithms|interface + impls|pricing, search|Open/Closed
emerald|Observer|~Notify on change|subject + observers|spot freed -> board|remember to unsubscribe
violet|Factory|~Hide creation|create(type)|no scattered new|when creation has logic
rose|Builder|~Complex construction|fluent chain|optional fields|5+ fields or optionals

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Pattern obsession** — forcing a Factory on a two-class hierarchy. Patterns are tools, not goals.
- **Singleton everywhere** — it's global state; overuse hurts testability.
- **Naming a pattern without its problem** — say *why* it's needed.
- **Builder for two fields** — a constructor or `record` is clearer; Builder shines with many optionals.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Master five: **Singleton, Strategy, Observer, Factory, Builder**.
- Know each one's **problem + one-line Java sketch**.
- **Strategy** + **Observer** appear most often in LLD.
- Always pair **problem → pattern**; skip patterns that don't earn their place.
- **Singleton** is global state — use sparingly.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
There are twenty-three classic Gang-of-Four patterns, but for fresher LLD interviews I focus on five that come up again and again. Singleton ensures exactly one shared instance of something, like a ParkingLot controller, using a private constructor and a getInstance method. Strategy lets me swap interchangeable algorithms behind an interface — that's the one I use for pricing or search, where the rules change but the surrounding code shouldn't. Observer is for event notification: when a spot is freed, the display boards that registered as observers get notified automatically, which keeps the spot decoupled from the display. Factory hides the choice of concrete class behind a create method, so I don't scatter new-statements and type checks around. And Builder gives a readable, fluent way to construct objects that have lots of optional fields, like a parking ticket.

For each one, I make sure I can state the problem it solves, sketch a one-line Java version, and — this is the part that impresses — say when not to use it. Strategy and Observer are the two I reach for most. But I'd be candid that patterns are tools, not goals. Forcing a Factory onto a trivial two-class hierarchy just adds indirection, Singletons are really global state and overusing them hurts testability, and a Builder for a two-field object is overkill when a constructor or a record reads better. So I name a pattern only when I can name the concrete problem it removes from my design.
